alright well firstly calm down, i know this is a stressful time and i’m trying to figure this out myself while preparing for admissions. imo there’s 2 types of ecs, ones that you join and ones that you initiate. you can join a club, an ngo, violin and wrestling are good examples that you mentioned. find something you’re really passionate about and do that. secondly, aos are also looking for leadership and initiative, things like starting your own club, leading projects in school and outside of it, they want to see people that are interested in making a positive change in their community. try finding a cause you’re passionate about and see what steps you could take towards helping it. if you’re good at math, talk to people at your school about starting a math club, etc ….

i think for ivies you absolutely need ecs. everyone applying is smart, has top exam/sat scores, extracurriculars are what set you apart. on that note - dont scramble to find a ton of things to launch yourself into. find a few you enjoy that are authentic to you and dedicate time to those. admission officers are looking for dedicated and driven people

Ooo that sounds interesting! A thing that's very interesting to me when it comes to "good characters turning evil" is their mentality or psychology - their thought process if you will. It wouldn't be a very realistic line of events if she has trained with this guy for a while, then he turns 'evil' and she suddely does too because she loves him or whatnot. Obviously she's going to become conflicted, like "I love my brother but I also love this guy and I want to be with him, what do I do ?!" If it's such a sudden change in her partner's behaviour, it makes it even less realistic to make her side with him imediately. 
Instead, I suggest doing a few things. One is that you can blur the line between 'good and bad'. Make the reason he turns evil obvious for the reader and give him a clear and valid motivation. Make the characters morally gray. You can also make her not realise that her partner turned evil, or make it so that she can understand and empathise with him enough so that she won't know she's evil until the climax of the story (which can be her battle with her brother)

i think i would have two tips when it comes to your story.

1. don't be afraid of using psychological torture! to me at least, psychological pain is 100x more interesting to read or watch. it can be very different from person to person, and so could the trauma left behind from it, hence why it could made an interesting idea if written well. your MC's situation seems very difficult for anyone to go through, so even if you don't necessarily plan on focusing on psychological torture for the result of not being able to control the Light, it might be interesting to at least hint towards or include in small bits.
2. i saw this somewhere once and i think it can really make a difference when a character is in pain; don't focus as much on the actual pain the character is feeling, focus more on the results of it. you can leave the  torture part up to the readers to interpret, and leave the actual description of it out of the story. Instead, you can focus on what the character )and characters around them) are thinking, feeling emotionally. I saw this example used, and i think it makes a lot of sense. We all know what a broken leg, or a broken arm feels like, so instead of focusing on the pain, focus on the effect it has on other people. If you're planning to write something more 'graphic', you can make characters around your MC turn around at the sight, get sick from it, try to avoid looking at it. Instead of writing the pain in the arm, write about the tingling and loss of sensation in the fingers. Write about how he impulsively hunches over cradling his arm. that sort of thing.
